meta.blurb: Ana watches about sixteen sunrises a day from a window on the space station, and her niece Lila has asked her to describe everything. Hurricanes, reefs and auroras glide past, and a thin blue line of air keeps everything alive.
meta.bible: Ana: a young astronaut, curious and brave, who spends about six months on the International Space Station. Lila: Ana's niece, who asked her to describe everything. The International Space Station: about 400 kilometres above Earth, almost as long as a football pitch, travelling at about 28,000 kilometres an hour and circling Earth in about ninety minutes, with about sixteen sunrises and sunsets a day. The Cupola: a dome with seven windows. Real places: Sahara, Nile, Amazon, Himalayas, Greenland, Antarctica, Aral Sea, Great Barrier Reef (about 2,300 kilometres long), Atlantic, Africa, Australia, Egypt, India, Asia, Pacific. Real events: Earthrise (Apollo 8, December 1968), the Blue Marble (Apollo 17, December 1972), the agreement of 1987 to protect the ozone layer. Key terms: Atmosphere, Ozone, Aurora, Hurricane, Phytoplankton, Terminator, Satellites, Capsule, Magnetic, Cupola, Orbit, Oxygen, Carbon, Moon, Sun, Milky Way, Apollo, Earthrise, Phosphorus, Wildfire, Wildfires, Volcano, Debris, Light pollution. The Earth is about 12,700 kilometres across; oceans cover about 71 percent; clouds cover about two thirds; the Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away; the Earth has warmed by a little more than one degree Celsius since the late 1800s. Every fact is real or marked as about; no invented numbers or studies. Voice: warm, wondering, clear.

beats.scene: Ana in an orange suit walks toward a tall white rocket at dawn
beats.summary: Ana is about to launch to the space station, hoping to see her whole home planet at once.

beats.scene: A rocket climbs on a column of fire as the sky turns black
beats.summary: The rocket climbs, and within minutes the sky turns black and Ana is in space.

beats.scene: The long white space station with big solar panels floats above the blue Earth
beats.summary: The International Space Station circles about four hundred kilometres above Earth and is as long as a football pitch.

beats.scene: Ana floats at a round window with seven panes that looks down at Earth
beats.summary: Ana floats to the Cupola, a window with seven panes, and sees Earth below.

beats.scene: A bright blue curve of Earth fills the window against black space
beats.summary: Seen from space, Earth is a curved ball with a bright blue colour, because the oceans cover about seventy-one percent of it.

beats.scene: A very thin glowing blue line of air hugs the curved edge of Earth
beats.summary: The atmosphere looks like a very thin blue line, though it is the air that keeps everything alive.

beats.scene: The station moves above blue ocean and brown land at great speed
beats.summary: The station travels about twenty-eight thousand kilometres an hour and circles Earth in about ninety minutes.

beats.scene: Golden sunlight spreads across the edge of Earth as the sun rises
beats.summary: The crew sees about sixteen sunrises and sunsets every day.

beats.scene: Half of Earth lies in shadow, with a sharp curved line to the day
beats.summary: Earth always has a day side and a night side, divided by a curved line that moves around the planet.

beats.scene: Swirls of white clouds cover large parts of the blue Earth
beats.summary: Clouds cover about two thirds of Earth at any moment.

beats.scene: A giant spiral hurricane with a dark round eye turns over the ocean
beats.summary: A hurricane looks like a huge spiral with a calm eye in the middle.

beats.scene: Flashes of lightning glow inside a dark storm cloud seen from above
beats.summary: Lightning flashes somewhere on Earth all the time, and from space the clouds seem to flicker.

beats.scene: A swirl of green and turquoise colour spreads across dark blue ocean
beats.summary: Tiny living things called phytoplankton make huge green patches in the ocean, and they produce a large share of the oxygen we breathe.

beats.scene: Pale turquoise water shows a long chain of reefs off a coastline
beats.summary: The Great Barrier Reef, about two thousand three hundred kilometres long, can be seen from space.

beats.scene: A thin green ribbon of river runs through a huge brown desert
beats.summary: The Nile is a thin green ribbon through the Sahara, and most people in Egypt live near it.

beats.scene: A huge yellow-brown cloud of dust blows from a desert out over the ocean
beats.summary: Dust from the Sahara blows across the Atlantic Ocean and falls on the Amazon, adding minerals to its soil.

beats.scene: A dark green forest is cut by a silver river with winding bends
beats.summary: The Amazon rainforest is a huge green area crossed by a winding river, and it holds an enormous variety of life.

beats.scene: Snow-covered mountain peaks rise in a long wall above brown plains
beats.summary: The Himalayas are the highest mountains on Earth, formed as India pushed into Asia.

beats.scene: A huge white ice sheet covers land beside a dark northern sea
beats.summary: Greenland and Antarctica are covered by huge ice sheets that hold most of the world's fresh water.

beats.scene: A satellite measures a melting glacier edge from above
beats.summary: Satellites show that the ice sheets are losing ice, and that sea levels are rising by a few millimetres a year.

beats.scene: A dark plume of smoke drifts across a green landscape from orange fires
beats.summary: Wildfire smoke can be seen from space, drifting for thousands of kilometres.

beats.scene: A grey ash plume spreads from a mountain on a small volcanic island
beats.summary: An erupting volcano sends ash plumes high into the air that can be seen from space.

beats.scene: A pale dry lakebed with a rusty ship lies in a sandy basin
beats.summary: The Aral Sea in Central Asia has shrunk dramatically since the 1960s because the rivers that fed it were used for farming.

beats.scene: Hundreds of perfect green circles of crops sit in a brown desert
beats.summary: Round green fields in dry places show that people water crops from the middle with long rotating pipes.

beats.scene: Grey city patches and dark roads seen from orbit
beats.summary: Cities are visible from orbit as grey patches, but the Great Wall of China cannot be seen with the naked eye.

beats.scene: Bright golden city lights shine across the dark night side of Earth
beats.summary: At night, city lights show where people live, and they trace coastlines, roads and rivers.

beats.scene: A wide city glow hides stars while a dark desert sky holds many stars
beats.summary: Artificial light spoils the view of the stars from many places, though remote areas still have dark skies.

beats.scene: A view of a continent from orbit with no visible lines between countries
beats.summary: From orbit, borders between countries cannot be seen, only the land, the sea and the rivers.

beats.scene: Green curtains of light ripple above the dark northern edge of Earth
beats.summary: An aurora is a glowing curtain of light near the poles, made when particles from the Sun hit the air.

beats.scene: Invisible curved lines surround Earth and bend a stream of particles
beats.summary: Earth has a magnetic field that bends most of the Sun's particles away from the surface.

beats.scene: A rainbow of thin glowing layers lies along the curved edge of Earth
beats.summary: At sunset, the atmosphere shows layers of colour at the edge of Earth, from orange to white to blue.

beats.scene: A faint blue layer high above Earth with a pale hole over the pole
beats.summary: The ozone layer protects life from the Sun's ultraviolet light, and after a hole appeared, countries agreed in 1987 to ban the chemicals that harmed it.

beats.scene: Tiny glinting satellites circle in lines above a curved Earth
beats.summary: Thousands of satellites circle Earth, giving us weather forecasts, maps, phone signals and television.

beats.scene: Small pieces of broken metal drift near a shining station above Earth
beats.summary: Space debris is a growing problem, and the station sometimes has to move to avoid pieces.

beats.scene: Four views of the same continent, green in summer and brown in winter
beats.summary: Satellites show how the colours of the land change with the seasons as plants grow and rest.

beats.scene: White vapour rises from the ocean and clouds drop rain over mountains
beats.summary: Water moves in a cycle: it rises from the sea, forms clouds, falls as rain and returns by rivers.

beats.scene: A thin glowing skin of green and blue hugs a great ball of rock
beats.summary: Life exists only in a thin layer at the surface of Earth, from the deep ocean to the high mountains.

beats.scene: A dark map of the world with small gathered clusters of light
beats.summary: Most people live on a small part of the land, in cities and along coasts and rivers.

beats.scene: A grey Moon surface with a blue and white Earth rising above the horizon
beats.summary: In 1968, the Apollo 8 astronauts were the first people to see Earth rise over the Moon, and they photographed it.

beats.scene: A whole round Earth with Africa in the centre, lit by the Sun
beats.summary: In 1972, the Apollo 17 crew photographed the whole sunlit Earth, in a picture called the Blue Marble.

beats.scene: A raised thumb covers a small blue Earth in a dark sky
beats.summary: From the Moon, about 384,000 kilometres away, Earth is small enough to cover with a thumb.

beats.scene: A small blue world among bright stars in black space
beats.summary: Earth is the only place known to have life, and astronomers search for other worlds with liquid water.

beats.scene: An astronaut pours drinking water from a bag next to a recycling machine
beats.summary: On the station, water, including sweat and urine, is cleaned and reused, as Earth recycles water naturally.

beats.scene: A smoky orange sky over a power station and a clear green forest
beats.summary: Carbon dioxide from burning fuels traps heat, and Earth has warmed by about one degree Celsius since the late 1800s.

beats.scene: A satellite looks down on a flooded river, a farm and a forest
beats.summary: Satellites help us watch forests, floods and farms, and they help rescue teams respond to disasters.

beats.scene: Ana floats quietly at the window and puts a hand on the glass
beats.summary: Many astronauts say that seeing Earth from space changed how they think about it and about each other.

beats.scene: A white capsule glows like a fireball as it falls through the thick air
beats.summary: Ana's capsule returns to Earth, and heat from the air glows around it as it slows down.

beats.scene: A capsule with a big striped parachute floats down onto a flat plain
beats.summary: A parachute opens and the capsule lands gently on the ground.

beats.scene: Ana sits with her bare feet on grass, holding a handful of earth
beats.summary: Back on Earth, Ana feels the weight of gravity and enjoys the smell of grass and rain.

beats.scene: Ana writes a letter by a window that looks onto a green garden
beats.summary: Ana writes to Lila, telling her to look up and to look after the planet that carries them all.

A1A2: Ana is an astronaut, and today she is going to space.
The rocket goes up fast, and the blue sky turns black.
Ana arrives at the station, which flies high above the Earth.
Ana floats to a round window and looks down at Earth.
From here, the Earth is a big blue ball.
At the edge of the Earth, Ana sees a thin blue line.
The station moves very fast and goes around Earth often.
Ana sees the sun rise about sixteen times each day.
Half of the Earth is in light, and half is in the dark.
White clouds cover a large part of the Earth.
Ana sees a big storm that looks like a white spiral.
At night, Ana sees lightning flash inside the clouds.
Tiny green plants in the sea can make big patches of colour.
Ana sees a long coral reef, and it is bright blue-green.
In a brown desert, Ana sees one long green river.
Wind carries dust from the desert across the sea.
Ana sees a very big green forest with a wide, winding river.
Ana sees the highest mountains in the world, white with snow.
Near the poles, Ana sees huge fields of white ice.
Satellites show that much of the ice is slowly melting.
Ana can see smoke from big forest fires far below.
A volcano sends a grey cloud high above the ocean.
A big lake in Asia has become much smaller since the 1960s.
In some deserts, Ana sees round green fields, like coins.
Ana can see big cities, but she cannot see the Great Wall.
At night, Ana sees cities shining like golden lights.
Cities are so bright that many people cannot see the stars.
From space, Ana cannot see the lines between countries.
Near the pole, Ana sees green curtains of light in the sky.
Earth has an invisible shield that pushes harmful particles away.
At sunset, the edge of the Earth shows bands of colour.
High in the air, a thin layer protects life from the Sun.
Thousands of satellites go around the Earth every day.
Old pieces of rocket are floating around the Earth.
The colours of the land change a little in each season.
Water goes up from the sea, makes clouds and then falls as rain.
All life on Earth lives in a very thin layer.
About eight billion people live on a small part of the Earth.
In 1968, astronauts saw the Earth rise over the Moon.
In 1972, other astronauts took a photograph of the whole Earth.
From the Moon, you could hide the Earth behind your thumb.
Earth is the only place we know that has life.
On the station, people clean and drink the same water again and again.
Burning coal, oil and gas adds a gas that warms the Earth.
Satellites help us to watch forests, floods and farms.
Many astronauts say that seeing Earth makes them feel different.
After six months, Ana returns to Earth in a small capsule.
A big parachute opens and slows the little capsule down.
Back on Earth, Ana feels very heavy and smells the grass.
Ana writes to Lila, and she says to look after the Earth.
B1B2: Ana has trained for years to become an astronaut, and today she will finally fly. She hopes to see something no map can ever show her, which is the whole Earth at once.
The engines roar, and the rocket pushes Ana back into her seat. Within about nine minutes the blue sky has faded to black, and she is in space.
The International Space Station flies about 400 kilometres above the ground. It is nearly as long as a football pitch, and it has been home to astronauts for many years.
After a few days, Ana floats to a special part of the station called the Cupola. It has seven windows, and through them she can see the whole planet below.
Most of what Ana sees is a deep blue. Oceans cover about 71 percent of the surface of the Earth, so a visitor from space would call it a water world.
At the edge of the planet, Ana sees a thin blue glow. That is the air, and it looks as thin as the skin of an apple, though all life on Earth depends on it.
The station moves at about 28,000 kilometres an hour, which is very fast. It goes all the way around the Earth in about ninety minutes.
Because the station circles the Earth so quickly, the crew sees about 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every day. Each one is a thin band of orange and blue that lasts only a short time.
The Sun always lights half of the Earth, while the other half is in the dark. The curved line between them moves slowly around the world as the planet turns.
Ana soon notices how many clouds there are around the planet. At any moment, they cover about two thirds of the planet, and they move in great swirls and long lines.
One day, Ana sees a hurricane, a giant storm that turns like a wheel. It has a calm round hole in the middle, called the eye, and the clouds wind around it.
On the night side of the planet, Ana sees flashes of lightning. Somewhere on Earth, lightning is flashing all the time, dozens of times every second.
In some places, the sea turns bright green or turquoise in great swirls. These are blooms of phytoplankton, tiny plant-like creatures that float near the surface and make oxygen.
Off the coast of Australia, Ana sees a long line of pale blue-green water. It is the Great Barrier Reef, which is about 2,300 kilometres long and is made by living coral.
Over Africa, Ana sees a thin green line running through a huge brown desert. It is the river Nile, and the green is farmland that the river water makes possible.
Sometimes a pale cloud of dust leaves the Sahara and crosses the Atlantic Ocean. Satellites show that it reaches South America, where it adds minerals to the rainforest soil.
Over South America, Ana sees a deep green carpet cut by a silver river. This is the Amazon rainforest, home to millions of kinds of plants, insects and animals.
Ana flies over the Himalayas, a long wall of white peaks. They are the highest mountains on Earth, and they are still rising slowly as India pushes into Asia.
Near the poles, Ana sees giant sheets of ice on the land. Greenland and Antarctica hold most of the fresh water in the world, and it is frozen there.
Satellites measure the ice every year, and the numbers are clear. Greenland and Antarctica are losing ice, which is one reason why the sea level is rising by a few millimetres each year.
From orbit, Ana can see the smoke of a large wildfire. It rises in a dark column, and then the wind spreads it into a long grey cloud that can drift for thousands of kilometres.
One day, Ana sees a volcano that has erupted. A tall grey column of ash and gas rises from the mountain, and the top spreads out like an umbrella.
Over Central Asia, Ana looks for the Aral Sea, which was once one of the biggest lakes in the world. Since the 1960s most of its water has gone, because people used its rivers for farms.
In dry places, Ana sees hundreds of perfect green circles. Each one is a farm field watered by a long pipe that turns around a point in the middle.
Cities are easy to see from the station, as large grey and brown patches. Many people believe that the Great Wall of China can be seen from space, but with the naked eye it cannot.
The night side of the Earth is full of lights. Cities glow like golden webs, and long chains of light follow the coasts, the roads and the rivers.
Bright city lights make the sky hazy, so many people can no longer see the stars. Ana remembers childhood nights in the countryside, when thousands of stars were clear.
On a map, countries are drawn with lines and bright colours. From the station, Ana looks for these lines, but she cannot see them, and there is only land and water.
One night, Ana flies through an aurora, a curtain of green light near the pole. It happens when charged particles from the Sun hit the air high above the Earth.
The Earth is like a giant magnet, and its magnetic field reaches far into space. It bends most of the particles from the Sun away, so they do not reach the ground.
At sunrise and sunset, Ana sees layers of colour at the edge of the Earth. They go from orange at the bottom to white in the middle and deep blue at the top.
High in the air, a layer of ozone blocks harmful light from the Sun. In the 1980s a hole appeared in it over Antarctica, so in 1987 countries agreed to stop using the chemicals that caused it.
Thousands of satellites circle the Earth all the time. They send us weather forecasts, maps, television and phone signals, so people use them every day without knowing it.
There are also thousands of pieces of broken rockets and old satellites in orbit, called space junk. Sometimes the station must move out of the way to avoid a piece.
Over the months, Ana sees the land change colour. In spring the north turns green as plants wake up, and in winter, snow covers much of it.
From orbit, Ana sees the water cycle at work. Water rises from the sea as vapour, forms clouds, falls as rain on the land and returns to the sea along rivers.
Life lives only in a thin layer, from the deepest ocean to the highest air. Compared with the whole planet, which is about 12,700 kilometres across, that layer is very thin indeed.
About eight billion people live on the Earth, but they are not spread out evenly. Most live in cities, near the coasts and beside rivers, and huge areas have almost nobody.
Ana often thinks about a famous photograph called Earthrise. In 1968, the astronauts of Apollo 8 were the first people to travel around the Moon, and they saw the Earth rising above its grey ground.
In 1972, the crew of Apollo 17 took another photograph, of the whole Earth in sunlight. Because it looks like a blue glass ball, it is called the Blue Marble.
The Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away from the Earth. From there, the whole planet looks so small that you can cover it with your thumb held out at arm's length.
Astronomers have found thousands of planets around other stars. However, so far, Earth is the only place we know that has life, and no other world has yet been shown to be like it.
On the station, nothing can be wasted at all. The crew's sweat, breath and even used water are cleaned and recycled so that they can drink them again.
When people burn coal, oil and gas, they add carbon dioxide to the air, and it traps heat. Measurements show that the Earth is now about one degree Celsius warmer than in the late 1800s.

Satellites do much more than take beautiful pictures of the Earth. They help farmers see which fields need water, they track forests and floods, and they help rescue teams find the people who need help.
Many astronauts describe the same feeling after seeing the Earth from space. They say it made them feel more connected to the planet and to the people on it.
After six months, Ana climbs into a small capsule and leaves the station. As it falls into the air, it meets so much friction that it glows orange and white with heat.
A big parachute opens and slows the falling capsule. With a gentle bump it lands on the flat ground, and rescue teams are already running toward it.
After six months of floating, Ana feels very heavy, and even lifting her arm is hard. Then the smell of the wet grass reaches her, and she laughs again.
Ana writes to Lila that the Earth is beautiful, and that it is also fragile. She asks her to look up at the sky, and then to look after the ground beneath her feet.
C1C2: Ana has spent nine years training to become an astronaut, and this morning she walks toward the rocket with her heart beating hard against her suit. She is not going to space to look at the stars, as most people suppose, but to turn around and look back at her own planet. Her young niece Lila has asked her to describe everything, and Ana has promised to do exactly that.

The engines roar and the whole rocket shakes as it pushes Ana hard back into her seat. The blue of the sky thins and darkens as she climbs, and in about nine minutes it has faded completely into black. Suddenly the shaking stops, her pencil floats up in front of her face, and she realises that she is in space.

The International Space Station travels about 400 kilometres above the ground, which is a distance you could drive in a few hours if only the road went upward. It is almost as long as a football pitch, and astronauts from many countries have lived aboard it without a break for more than twenty years. To Ana, as she drifts through its hatch, it feels like a small, humming village hanging in the dark.

After a few days of getting used to floating, Ana makes her way to the Cupola, a small dome with seven windows that is the best viewing seat on the station. She holds a handrail, turns her face to the glass and sees the planet moving silently below her. For some minutes she cannot say a single word, and then she begins to laugh.

Most of what Ana sees below her is a deep, glittering blue, because oceans cover about 71 percent of the planet's surface. A visitor arriving from another star might reasonably decide that this world should be called Water, not Earth. The land, with all its cities and farms and mountains, turns out to be the smaller part of the picture.

Along the curved edge of the planet, Ana sees a thin, glowing blue band that fades into the blackness of space. That fragile layer is the atmosphere, and compared with the size of the Earth it is about as thin as the skin on an apple. Almost everything alive depends on it for air, warmth and protection, and from up here it looks astonishingly easy to damage.

To stay up, the station must move sideways at about 28,000 kilometres an hour, so quickly that it keeps falling around the curve of the Earth without ever landing. A full circle of the planet takes only about ninety minutes, which means that Ana can have breakfast over Africa and look down on the Pacific Ocean before she has finished her tea. Continents slide past her window like pages of an enormous book, turned one after another without a pause.

Because the station circles the Earth every ninety minutes or so, the crew sees about sixteen sunrises and sixteen sunsets in a single day. Each one begins as a thin band of orange and deep blue along the horizon and then bursts into dazzling white light within a few seconds. Ana soon discovers that the ordinary idea of morning and evening does not mean very much in orbit.

At any moment, half of the Earth is lit by the Sun while the other half lies in shadow, and the curved line between them is called the terminator. It races steadily westward over the oceans and the continents as the planet spins, so that morning is always arriving somewhere and night is always beginning somewhere else. From the station, Ana can watch that slow tide of light and dark as it sweeps around the world.

Ana soon notices how many clouds there are, and how rarely she sees a clear view of any one place. At any moment about two thirds of the planet is covered by them, arranged in great spirals, long streets and soft, scattered patches. They are a reminder that the water of the Earth is never still, and that the sky is a busy place.

One day she sees a hurricane below her, a vast white wheel of cloud turning slowly over the warm ocean. In the centre is a dark, calm opening called the eye, and the clouds spiral around it in perfect arms that stretch for hundreds of kilometres. From above it looks beautiful and almost peaceful, though she knows that on the ground it can be fierce and frightening.

On the night side of the planet, storm clouds flicker from within, as though someone were switching lamps on and off inside them. Scientists estimate that lightning flashes somewhere on Earth dozens of times every second, and from the Cupola Ana can see a whole region flickering at once. It makes her think of the planet as something alive, with a nervous system of electric light.

In some places the dark blue sea breaks into swirls of bright green and turquoise, as if a painter had stirred the water with a brush. These are blooms of phytoplankton, microscopic floating organisms that use sunlight to grow, and together they produce a large share of the oxygen that we breathe, perhaps about half. Every second breath Lila takes may owe something to creatures too small to see.

Off the north-eastern coast of Australia, a long ribbon of pale turquoise stretches across the dark water, and Ana knows at once what it is. The Great Barrier Reef runs for about 2,300 kilometres, and it was built over thousands of years by tiny animals called corals. It is the largest structure made by living things, and it can be seen clearly from orbit.

Crossing north Africa, Ana sees a thin green line cutting through an enormous sweep of brown and gold. It is the Nile, and the narrow strip of green on either side is farmland that exists only because the river waters it. Most people in Egypt live within that ribbon, which shows very clearly how close life can come to depending on a single source of water.

From time to time, a great pale cloud of dust lifts off the Sahara and drifts west across the Atlantic Ocean, and Ana can follow it for hours. Satellite measurements show that a good deal of it settles over the Amazon rainforest thousands of kilometres away, where it adds minerals such as phosphorus to the soil. The desert and the rainforest, it turns out, are quietly connected by the wind, across a whole ocean.

Over South America the land turns into a deep green carpet crossed by a wide silver river that twists back and forth like a loosened ribbon. This is the Amazon, the largest rainforest on Earth and home to an enormous number of species, many of which have not yet been described by science. Even from four hundred kilometres up, Ana can see how the forest seems to breathe.

Ana crosses the Himalayas, a vast wall of white peaks that rises above the brown plains of Asia like a frozen wave. They are the highest mountains on Earth, and they are still growing by a few millimetres a year as the land of India presses slowly into the rest of the continent. From orbit the whole range looks wrinkled, as though the surface of the planet had been squeezed.

Near the poles, Ana looks down on the two giant ice sheets of Greenland and Antarctica, white deserts that gleam in the sunlight. Together they hold most of the fresh water on the planet, locked up in ice that is in places more than two kilometres thick. They look permanent and still, but the scientists who study them know that they are changing.

Satellites now measure the height of the ice from orbit, year after year, and the results are clear. Both Greenland and Antarctica are losing ice, and the melting water is one of the reasons why sea levels are rising by a few millimetres every year. A few millimetres may not sound like much, yet it adds up over decades and puts low coastal cities at risk.

Over a dry forest region, Ana sees a column of dark smoke rising from a line of small orange flames. The wind soon bends it into a long grey veil that can drift for thousands of kilometres, sometimes darkening the sky of a city far away. Fires are a natural part of many landscapes, but hotter, drier weather is making some of them larger and more dangerous.

One morning, a volcano on a small island has erupted, and Ana sees its plume of ash and gas rise like a tall grey tree from the sea. The top of the column spreads wide in the upper air, where winds carry the fine ash around the world. Great eruptions can even cool the climate for a year or two, which is a reminder that the planet's interior is still restless.

Over Central Asia, Ana searches for the Aral Sea, and finds mostly pale, dry land where a great lake used to be. Since the 1960s the rivers that fed it have been diverted to irrigate cotton and other crops, and the lake has shrunk to a small fraction of its former size. Satellite photographs from different years, placed side by side, make the loss easy to see.

In some of the driest parts of the world, hundreds of perfect green circles lie scattered across the brown sand like coins on a table. Each one is a farm field watered by a long, rotating pipe that draws water from deep underground, and the circles are among the clearest marks that humans leave on the landscape. They show how people have learned to make crops grow in places that nature left empty.

By day, cities appear as large grey-brown patches with a pattern of roads running out of them like the spokes of a wheel. Many people believe that the Great Wall of China can be seen from space with the naked eye, but Ana and her crewmates agree that it cannot, since it is long but extremely narrow. What shows most clearly from up here is not great monuments but ordinary human settlements.

On the night side of the Earth, Ana looks down upon a glittering map made entirely of electric light. Cities glow like golden webs, and chains of smaller lights trace the coastlines, the highways and the river valleys, while the sea and the empty land lie perfectly black. It is a portrait of where people live, drawn each evening without anyone planning it.

The glow of a big city floats above it like a dome of light, and Ana knows that beneath it many people have never seen the Milky Way. Light pollution has taken the night sky away from a large part of humanity, and she remembers how thousands of stars once crowded the dark sky above her grandmother's village. A few places, such as deserts and remote mountains, still keep their darkness, and Ana hopes that they always will.

On a map, every country is drawn in its own colour and enclosed by a neat black line, but Ana searches the land below and finds no such lines. Occasionally a fence or a change in farming can reveal a border, yet most of them are invisible, as though the planet were a single piece. It strikes her as odd that something so important on the ground should vanish from the sky.

One night, the station seems to skim through a vast curtain of shimmering green light that ripples above the northern edge of the planet. This is an aurora, which appears when charged particles streaming from the Sun strike the thin air high above the poles and make it glow. Ana had seen photographs all her life, but she has never imagined that the light could be so soft and so alive.

The Earth behaves like an enormous magnet, because of the churning liquid metal deep inside its core, and its magnetic field reaches far out into space. This invisible shield bends most of the charged particles from the Sun away from the planet, so that only a small share can reach the atmosphere and make the aurora. Without that shield, life on the surface would have a much harder time, and the surface would be exposed to far more radiation.

Just before sunrise, Ana sees the edge of the Earth glowing in layers of colour, with orange near the surface, a band of white above it, and a deepening blue that fades into black. The bands show the different layers of the atmosphere, and the lowest and thickest of them holds most of the air and almost all the weather. Above the lowest layer, the air thins rapidly, and there is hardly anything left at all.

High above the weather, a thin layer of ozone gas absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light. In the 1980s scientists found that a hole was opening in it over Antarctica, caused by certain chemicals, and in 1987 the countries of the world agreed to phase those chemicals out. The layer is now slowly recovering, which Ana thinks is a hopeful story of what nations can do together.

Thousands of satellites now circle the Earth, and Ana sometimes sees one flash past like a tiny, fast-moving star. They carry television, telephone and navigation signals, and they watch the weather, so that most people use them many times a day without ever thinking about them. The planet is wrapped in a quiet web of machines that most people never see.

Orbit is not empty, for it also contains thousands of pieces of old rockets, dead satellites and tiny flecks of paint, all travelling at tremendous speed. Even a small fragment can do serious damage at that velocity, and the station sometimes has to fire its engines to dodge a piece. Ana finds it sobering that humans have managed to make rubbish in space as well as on the ground.

Over the months, Ana watches the colours of the land change in a slow, great rhythm. In the north, the green of spring spreads outward as the plants wake, then it fades to gold and brown in autumn, and snow finally closes over it. Satellite records show that this yearly pulse is so strong that the planet seems almost to breathe in and out.

From orbit, Ana can see the water cycle operating on a scale that no classroom diagram could convey. The sun lifts vapour from the oceans, the wind carries it inland as cloud, and the rain that falls on the mountains gathers into rivers that find their way back to the sea. The same water has been going around for billions of years, and some of it was once in the bodies of dinosaurs.

All the life that we know about exists in a very thin layer at the surface of the planet, reaching from the deepest ocean trenches up to the highest mountains and clouds. Measured against the Earth's width of about 12,700 kilometres, that living layer is only a few kilometres deep, scarcely thicker than a coat of paint on a ball. Everything alive, including every plant, animal and person, is crowded into this narrow band.

About eight billion people now live on the Earth, but they are spread very unevenly across its surface. Most of them crowd into cities, river valleys and coastal plains, while vast areas of desert, ice, forest and mountain are almost empty. From the station, Ana is struck by how much of the planet remains wild, and by how small the human footprint is in many places.

In her free time, Ana often thinks about a famous photograph called Earthrise, which was taken long before she was born. In December 1968, the three astronauts of Apollo 8 became the first people to travel around the Moon, and as their spacecraft came out from behind it they saw a blue and white Earth rising above the grey, lifeless horizon. They had flown all that way to study the Moon, yet it was the sight of home that took their breath away.

A few years later, in December 1972, the crew of Apollo 17 took a photograph of the entire Earth fully lit by the Sun behind them, with Africa in the middle and white Antarctica at the bottom. People soon named it the Blue Marble, because the planet looks like a glass ball, and it became one of the most widely reproduced pictures in history. It has been printed on posters and school books around the world ever since.

The Moon is about 384,000 kilometres away, and from there the whole Earth shrinks to a size you can hide behind your thumb at arm's length. Every ocean, every mountain range and every city would fit inside that small blue disc. Ana finds it hard to imagine, and yet she knows that every astronaut who has made the journey has described exactly this feeling.

Astronomers have now discovered thousands of planets circling other stars, and some of them lie at a distance where liquid water might be possible. Even so, Earth remains the only place where life is definitely known to exist, and no other world has yet been shown to be much like it. That does not mean that nobody is out there, but it does mean that we should take good care of this one.

On the station, nothing can be wasted, because every litre of water and every breath of air has to be brought up from the ground at great expense. Machines collect the crew's sweat, breath and used water and clean it so that it can be drunk again, and Ana soon gets used to the idea. Back on Earth, she reflects, nature does exactly the same thing, on a much larger scale and without the machines.

When people burn coal, oil and gas, they release carbon dioxide, a gas that traps heat in the atmosphere, and its amount in the air has risen sharply since the nineteenth century. Measurements from thousands of instruments, many of them on satellites, show that the Earth has warmed by a little more than one degree Celsius since the late 1800s. The warming is small in number, but its effects on ice, seas and weather are already visible.

Satellites do far more than take beautiful pictures, for they have become some of the most useful instruments we have. They help farmers see which fields are thirsty, track the loss of forests, warn of coming floods and guide rescue teams after earthquakes and storms. Looking at the planet as a whole, it turns out, is one of the best ways of looking after it.

Many astronauts describe a very similar feeling after seeing the Earth from above, a mixture of awe, calm and responsibility. They say that the planet looks so small and so fragile that ordinary quarrels seem less important, and they come back wanting to protect it. Ana, resting her hand lightly against the cold glass of the Cupola, finds that she feels exactly the same.

After six months in orbit, Ana climbs into a small capsule and leaves the station, firing its engines to drop out of orbit. As the capsule plunges into the thickening air at tremendous speed, friction heats the outside until it glows orange and white behind the window. A heat shield takes the full blast of it, and Ana, strapped in tightly, feels the weight of gravity returning.

Lower in the sky, a pair of parachutes opens and the capsule swings gently down, slowing from a terrifying speed to a walking pace. It touches the flat plain with a soft thump, and within minutes the rescue team has opened the hatch to let in the first fresh air that Ana has breathed for half a year. She can hear the wind in the grass and the voices of the people running toward her.

After half a year of floating, Ana finds that her own arms feel as heavy as sandbags, and standing up needs all of her effort. Then the scent of wet grass and earth reaches her, a smell that she had not realised she would miss, and tears of happiness fill her eyes. Nothing in orbit, however magnificent, was quite as wonderful as the ordinary air of home.

In her letter to Lila, Ana says that the Earth is the most beautiful thing she has ever seen, and also the most fragile. She explains that from space it looks like a single living thing, with no walls and no spare parts, carrying everyone aboard through the dark. Look up at the sky as often as you like, she writes, but never forget that the most important thing in the whole universe, for us, is the ground under our feet.
